units.title: Logic and Proof Techniques
topics: Which proof technique should I try?
Eight uses of logic in computing

sections.title: Which proof technique should I try?
Eight uses of logic in computing

summary: Propositions combine through connectives; the truth table decides equivalence, tautology or contradiction.
Quantifiers extend logic to properties of many objects; negation swaps ∀ and ∃.
Valid arguments chain inference rules; invalid ones commit fallacies.
Proof techniques are templates; choose by the shape of the statement.

units.title: Sets, Relations and Functions
topics: Three kinds of function in one picture
Eight uses of sets, relations and functions

sections.title: Three kinds of function in one picture
Eight uses of sets, relations and functions

summary: Sets and bit strings: union, intersection and complement are the logical operators applied to membership.
Relations capture structure (equivalence → partitions, order → posets); closures add forced pairs.
Functions classified as injective, surjective, bijective; counting uses powers, falling factorials and inclusion–exclusion.
Cardinality separates countable from uncountable infinities, with consequences for computability.

units.title: Counting: Permutations, Combinations and the Pigeonhole Principle
topics: Pascal's triangle: all the binomial coefficients in one picture

sections.title: Pascal's triangle: all the binomial coefficients in one picture

summary: Product and sum rules solve most counting problems; subtract overlaps with inclusion–exclusion.
Order matters → permutations; order does not → combinations; repetition changes the formula.
The binomial theorem links combinations to powers and subsets.
The pigeonhole principle proves existence without finding the object.

units.title: Induction, Recursion and Recurrence Relations
topics: The recursion tree of merge sort
Eight uses of induction and recursion

sections.title: The recursion tree of merge sort
Eight uses of induction and recursion

summary: Induction proves infinitely many statements with two finite checks; strong induction is the right tool when the step needs several earlier cases.
Recursive definitions give structures and programs; structural induction proves their properties.
Linear recurrences are solved through the characteristic equation; non-homogeneous ones add a particular solution.
The master theorem gives the cost of divide-and-conquer algorithms at a glance.

units.title: Graphs and Trees
topics: Weighted graphs: shortest paths and spanning trees
Eight uses of graphs and trees

sections.title: Weighted graphs: shortest paths and spanning trees
Eight uses of graphs and trees

summary: Graphs are vertices and edges; degree, paths and connectivity answer structural questions, and the handshake lemma constrains degrees.
Euler's theorem decides Euler circuits by degrees; Hamilton circuits have no simple test.
Planarity and colouring have formulas and applications in scheduling.
Dijkstra gives shortest paths and Kruskal/Prim give minimum spanning trees.
Trees are acyclic connected graphs; traversals, search trees and Huffman codes are their main uses.

units.title: Number Theory, Modular Arithmetic and Algebraic Structures
topics: Clock arithmetic and the RSA message path
Eight uses of number theory and algebraic structures

sections.title: Clock arithmetic and the RSA message path
Eight uses of number theory and algebraic structures

summary: The Euclidean algorithm computes gcds quickly and the extended version yields inverses.
Modular arithmetic lets us compute with remainders; Fermat, Euler and the CRT are its workhorses.
RSA turns the difficulty of factoring into public-key encryption.
Groups, rings and fields classify structures by their axioms; Boolean algebras unify logic, sets and circuits.

Boolean functions, floor and ceiling, and relational databases

Integer representations and the algorithms of arithmetic

sections.title: Proof methods that were missing, and mistakes in proofs
Boolean functions, floor and ceiling, and relational databases
Well-ordering, strong induction and the correctness of recursive algorithms
Integer representations and the algorithms of arithmetic
Counting objects that are not all different, and generating permutations
Graph models, isomorphism, matching and the travelling salesman problem

summary: Vacuous and trivial proofs, proofs by cases, existence and uniqueness proofs and counterexamples complete the proof toolbox; the common mistakes are the converse and inverse errors, circular reasoning and division by zero.
Floor and ceiling convert real numbers to integers; Boolean functions are maps from bit strings to bits; n-ary relations are the mathematics of database tables with selection, projection and join.
Well-ordering is equivalent to induction, and recursive algorithms are proved correct by induction on the input size.
Integers are stored in base 2 and written in base 8 or 16; arithmetic uses carry, shift-and-add, division with remainder and repeated squaring.
Arrangements with identical objects divide by the factorials of the repeats; next-permutation and combination generation list objects in lexicographic order.
Probability adds conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, expectation, variance, randomized algorithms and the hashing collision analysis.
Graphs model many real systems; isomorphism, matching and the travelling salesman problem show where graph questions become easy or hard.
